Session 3 · 3.1 Inside the back end: a Python web server · 1/2Book ↗

A complete dynamic web server

from flask import Flask
from datetime import datetime
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/hours")
def hours():
    if 7 <= datetime.now().hour < 18:
        return "<p>We are <b>open</b> right now!</p>"
    return "<p>We are closed. Back at 7 a.m.</p>"

app.run(port=5000)
  • Flask is a framework: it handles the routine parts of being a server
  • Each route connects a path to a function; the function's return value is the response
Session 3 · 3.1 Inside the back end: a Python web server · 2/2Book ↗

Localhost, ports, and templates

  • localhost means "this computer": browser and server on the same laptop
  • A port is a numbered door: 443 for HTTPS, 5000 or 3000 for testing
  • Two visitors a minute apart at 5:59 and 6:00 see different pages: that is "dynamic"
  • Real back ends fill in templates (HTML with blanks) rather than gluing strings
Session 3 · 3.2 APIs and JSON · 1/4Book ↗

The menu is the API

  • An API is the defined set of requests a program accepts and the answers it gives
  • Callers are often programs, not people: page JavaScript, a mobile app, a partner, an AI
  • Each address in an API is an endpoint; answers come back as data, not designed pages
Session 3 · 3.2 APIs and JSON · 2/4Book ↗

JSON: the common tongue of the web

{
  "products": [
    {"id": 1, "name": "Sourdough loaf", "price": 7.5, "in_stock": true},
    {"id": 2, "name": "Rye bread", "price": 6.0, "in_stock": false}
  ]
}
  • Curly braces: named values. Square brackets: lists. Almost exactly a Python dictionary and list

Verbs: nouns in the URL, verbs in the method

MethodMeaningBakery exampleCRUD
GETReadGET /api/productsRead

PUT / PATCHUpdatePATCH /api/orders/88Update

This style is REST. Most business software is CRUD screens over a database.
Session 3 · 3.2 APIs and JSON · 4/4Book ↗

APIs in both directions

  • You offer an API to your front ends and partners; you consume third-party APIs (Stripe, Claude, email) instead of building
  • An API key identifies your account to a third party. It lives on your server, never in front-end code
Session 3 · 3.3 Why every product needs a database · 1/2Book ↗

Why not just save to a file?

  • Many writers at once: two customers buying the last challah must not both succeed
  • Speed at scale: an index finds one order in ten million in milliseconds
  • Reliability: a transaction is all-or-nothing, even if the power fails halfway
  • Questions: "who ordered rye three times last quarter?" is one line
  • The database is a separate program (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite) your back end talks to
Session 3 · 3.3 Why every product needs a database · 2/2Book ↗

The relational model

  • Tables of rows and columns; each table holds one kind of thing
  • Primary key: the unique ID of a row. Foreign key: a column pointing at another table's row
  • Change Dana's email once; every order she placed reflects it
The table design (the schema) is really a design of the business.
Session 3 · 3.4 SQL by example · 1/4Book ↗

Reading: SELECT

SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE city = 'Boston';

SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS how_many
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;
  • SELECT picks columns, FROM picks the table, WHERE filters rows
  • COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX are aggregate functions: every dashboard is a stack of these
Session 3 · 3.4 SQL by example · 2/4Book ↗

Combining tables: JOIN

SELECT customers.name, products.name, orders.quantity
FROM orders
JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id
JOIN products  ON orders.product_id  = products.product_id
WHERE orders.status = 'placed';
  • A JOIN stitches rows together using the keys, so "Dana Levi, Rye bread, 1" comes out readable
Session 3 · 3.4 SQL by example · 3/4Book ↗

Writing: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, product_id, quantity, status)
VALUES (3, 1, 2, 'placed');

UPDATE orders SET status = 'ready' WHERE order_id = 88;

DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 89;
  • DELETE FROM orders; with no WHERE deletes every order in the company
  • CREATE TABLE defines columns, data types, keys, and constraints the database enforces
Session 3 · 3.4 SQL by example · 4/4Book ↗

Which database?

ProductTypeTypical use
SQLiteRelational, single filePrototypes, phone apps; built into Python
PostgreSQLRelational serverDefault for new web products
MySQLRelational serverOlder web products, WordPress
SQL Server, OracleRelational serverLarge enterprises, finance
MongoDBDocument (NoSQL)Flexible data shapes
RedisKey-value, in memoryCaching, sessions
You will not write SQL in this course. You will read it and say what it does.
Session 3 · 3.5 Beyond tables: NoSQL and ORMsBook ↗

NoSQL and ORMs

  • NoSQL relaxes the rules: a document database (MongoDB) stores JSON-like records with any fields
  • Price of flexibility: fewer guarantees, clumsier joins. Rule of thumb: start relational
  • An ORM lets Python treat rows as objects and writes the SQL behind the scenes
  • Claude Code will almost certainly use an ORM; the concepts underneath are unchanged
Session 3 · 3.6 The three-tier architecture · 1/3Book ↗

Presentation, application, data

  • Presentation tier: the front end in the browser or app
  • Application tier: the back-end program; where business logic lives (prices, permissions, workflows)
  • Data tier: the database
Session 3 · 3.6 The three-tier architecture · 2/3Book ↗

One order through three tiers

Session 3 · 3.6 The three-tier architecture · 3/3Book ↗

Three consequences

  • The browser never touches the database directly; the back end checks identity and applies rules
  • Each tier can be changed independently: redesign the front end without touching the data
  • Each tier can live on different hardware: today one laptop, tomorrow ten servers (Session 4)
Anything in the browser can be altered by the user. Rules and secrets live on the server.
